title: Define staff dining and patient meals separately
focus: A staff cafeteria, visitor service and patient meal operation have different requirements and should not be combined into an undefined brief. For any patient-related request, the responsible clinical and operational teams must specify the requirements and assess the proposed arrangements. Therapeutic diets need an approved clinical brief and appropriate capabilities before a commitment can be made. Begin with the site, intended users, meal volumes and required documentation so the discussion remains specific and realistic.

sections.title: Map the operation by service and shift
paragraphs: Start by separating staff dining, visitor food service and any patient meal request. For each, record the expected daily volumes, operating hours and available facilities. A cafeteria supporting a night shift has different access and replenishment needs from a visitor counter serving a shorter daytime window.

Bring procurement and facilities into the initial assessment. Identify where food would be prepared, received, held and served, together with the equipment and staffing already available. Site access, cleaning, maintenance and waste responsibilities should be assigned in the proposal so the food-service scope can be evaluated as a complete operation.

If patient meals are requested, include the responsible clinical and operational teams from the beginning. Their approved requirements determine the specification against which a proposed provider is assessed. Suitability, documentation and responsibilities must be confirmed before patient meal service is accepted or a launch date is agreed.

sections.title: Keep clinical decisions with the responsible team
paragraphs: The hospital defines the clinical dietary requirements for patient meals. The catering brief should use its approved specifications, identifiers and review process, with the relevant clinical or dietetic responsibility named. A condition name alone does not give a culinary team enough information to determine a suitable meal.

Any therapeutic diet or texture-modified request needs explicit assessment of the proposed production and service arrangements. The responsible healthcare professionals approve the specifications; the provider confirms whether it can meet them. Changes and substitutions follow the hospital process rather than an informal decision at the kitchen pass.

Staff and visitor menus have their own dietary information and service plan. Keep these clearly distinguished from patient meal instructions. Agree how ingredients, labels and handovers are managed for each service, and identify the contact who can resolve questions before food is released or a change is made.

sections.title: Review the proposal as an operating agreement
paragraphs: Compare providers against the same scope, meal volumes and service hours. Food, staffing, equipment, transport and any specialist requirements should be identifiable in the proposal. Confirm what the facility supplies and which costs depend on actual daily demand, since these assumptions can materially affect the operating budget.

Procurement should review the documentation and approval conditions together with the commercial terms. Include the required reporting, escalation contacts, trial arrangements and responsibilities for maintaining the service. A staff dining trial may test practical operation; it does not automatically establish suitability for a separate patient meal scope.

Before launch, agree how performance will be reviewed. Useful operational measures include delivery timing, order accuracy, service availability and feedback from the responsible site team. Any clinical assessment remains with the hospital. The contract and approved operating plan provide the shared reference for changes during the arrangement.
